decisions.0: King-ten suited opens from the small blind every time: only the big blind is left to act, and a suited king is ahead of its range often enough.
decisions.1: Facing the big blind's 3-bet, king-ten suited usually calls: it is too good to fold and plays well after the flop. A 4-bet now and then is fine too.
decisions.2: You have an open-ended straight draw, any ace or nine, plus an overcard: a strong draw. Calling sees the turn cheaply; raising can win the pot now and still has many outs if called. Both are about equally good, and calling is more common. Folding is the mistake: you need 27% and you win about half the time.
decisions.3: The five misses you. Out of position with a draw, checking lets you see the river; when you check, the big blind checks behind almost half the time and gives you a free card. A big bet would fold its weak hands and get called by its strong ones, which costs 3.66 bb.
decisions.4: Your straight draw missed, and king-high now wins only against the big blind's own misses. Your range as a whole is strong here, but this hand is not: a bet would fold the hands you beat and get called by pairs. Checking keeps the showdown value; betting half the pot costs 1.12 bb.

takeaway: When a draw misses, a hand that can still win at showdown checks; bluff with hands that cannot win any other way.
